Terminology is swapped. In mathematics a strictly increasing sequence only requires each value to be greater than the one before, so 1 2 5 7 8 9 32 33 34 is strictly increasing too; 'monotonically (non-strictly) increasing' allows repeats. precise_version: Strictly increasing means every new ID is larger than all earlier ones (gaps allowed); gap-free 1, 2, 3, ... is a stronger property usually called sequential or consecutive.

Common clock crystals do not run faster when hot and slower when cold. The main cost is randomness, not just size: RFC 9562 says non-time-ordered UUIDs such as v4 'have poor database-index locality', so inserts scatter across the B-tree. 16 bytes is 4x a 4-byte INT but only 2x a BIGINT, the realistic comparison (Snowflake-style IDs are 8 bytes). Index size also does not scale linearly with key size, because entries carry row pointers and page overhead (the teacher hedges this in L-0154). Snowflake is only roughly ordered: right. But auto-increment does not give strict order either. InnoDB's default interleaved mode interleaves values across concurrent statements, rolled-back values leave gaps, and a transaction holding a lower ID can commit after one holding a higher ID. For a strict ledger order you need a single writer, or a sequence assigned at commit under serialization.
precise_version: Snowflake IDs are only roughly time-ordered. A single database's auto-increment gives unique, increasing values per insert, but concurrent transactions can commit out of ID order.

note: Banks do prefer a single authoritative sequence over Snowflake-style IDs, but as L-0294's note explains, plain auto-increment is not commit order under concurrency. Ledgers usually serialize postings per account.

Not every queue gives this. SQS standard queues are at-least-once: a copy may be delivered again, so a range could be handed to two servers and produce duplicate IDs unless consumers dedupe (or you use exactly-once processing such as FIFO deduplication). DynamoDB atomic counters and Redis INCRBY are fine: a retried increment overcounts, wasting a range but never duplicating one.
